body: Rushing ahead can become a habit so quiet you stop seeing it. For about ninety days, these notes will invite you back into the hours you are actually living.
There is nothing to change yet. Simply catch the moments when your body is in one place and your mind has already left for the next.
Autopilot is not a flaw. It is your brain saving effort. The aim here is simply to choose when to switch it off.
Which parts of your day pass without leaving any memory at all? A commute, a shower, a meal? Just take note of them.
When did you last taste the first sip of a drink properly? Many people go years without doing so. That is worth knowing, not worrying about.
Rushing often hides a belief that life starts later, once the list is done. See whether that belief shows up in you this week.
Your attention has a texture. Some hours it is scattered, some hours it settles. Begin to get curious about which is which.
Being present is not about feeling calm. It is about being here, even for the boring or awkward bits.
Watch how often your hand reaches for your phone in a pause. No judgement. The reach itself is useful information.
Rehearsing tomorrow's conversations, replaying yesterday's: both pull you out of now. Spot which one is your favourite.
In conversation, where does your mind wander? Planning your reply, checking the time, drifting off? Simply observe the pattern.
Your senses are always in the present. Sound, touch and smell cannot be anywhere else, which makes them a handy way back.
Some rushing is necessary. Trains leave on time. The question is how much of the hurry is real and how much is habit.
Multitasking often feels productive while making everything a little thinner. At a few random points, count how many things you are doing at once.
Good moments slip past when attention is elsewhere. Think back over this week: which pleasant moment do you barely remember living?
Presence comes and goes for everyone, including people who meditate for hours. Drifting off is normal; coming back is the skill.
Pay attention to your breathing when you feel hurried. Is it shallower or quicker? The body often knows before the mind admits it.
Waiting is a good clue. Queues, kettles, loading screens. How do you feel in those gaps, and what do you usually do with them?
Ask yourself what you are hoping to reach by always moving on. Sometimes the answer is surprising, sometimes it is simply relief.
A present life is not automatically a slower life. It is one where you are around for whatever pace you choose.
Three weeks of simply watching is already a form of presence. From tomorrow, small daily experiments begin.
Drink your first cup of tea or coffee without a screen. Feel the warmth of the mug, the smell, the first taste, then carry on with your day.
Pick one doorway you walk through often. Each time you cross it, take one slow breath and feel your feet on the floor.
Eat the first three mouthfuls of one meal slowly, putting your fork down between each. After that, eat however you like.
On a short walk, name five things you have never properly looked at before. A crack in the pavement, a colour, a sign.
Choose one task and do only that for ten minutes. Close other tabs, silence alerts, and see what single-tasking feels like.
In your next conversation, let the other person finish completely, then pause for one breath before replying.
Wash your hands slowly once, paying attention to the temperature of the water and the slippery feel of the soap.
Stand at a window for one minute and listen. Count how many different sounds you can pick out, near and far.
Make your bed slowly and deliberately, smoothing each corner with care. A two-minute chore can become a small moment of arrival.
When something pleasant happens, however small, stay with it for an extra ten seconds before moving on. Let it land.
Set a gentle reminder for mid-afternoon. When it goes off, ask yourself where your attention is right now, and where your body is.
Walk the last hundred metres of any journey a little slower than usual. Arrive rather than simply turn up.
During a shower, follow the sensation of water on your shoulders for one full minute instead of planning the day.
Put your phone face down and out of reach during one meal with someone. Look at them when they speak.
Choose an ordinary object, a key or a spoon, and study it for sixty seconds as if you had never seen one before.
Before opening your inbox, take three slow breaths and decide on one thing you want to give your full attention to first.
Listen to one piece of music all the way through without doing anything else. Lying down while you listen counts.
When you catch yourself rushing, deliberately slow your next movement by half. Close the drawer gently, set the cup down softly.
Ask someone a follow-up question about something they said, rather than moving the conversation on to your own news.
Spend two minutes outside looking up at the sky. Clouds, light, birds, aircraft, whatever happens to be there.
Brush your teeth with your other hand. The awkwardness wakes up your attention in a way routine never does.
At a red light or in a queue, resist reaching for anything. Feel your weight, your breath, the space around you.
Before bed, write down three things you smelled during the day. It is harder than it sounds, and that is rather the point.
Turn off one non-essential notification for good. Just one. See whether you miss it by the end of the week.
While the kettle boils, keep your eyes on it and listen to it change pitch as it heats. A tiny ninety-second retreat.
On your next phone call, close everything else on your screen. Give the voice your whole attention, as if they were in the room.
Peel a piece of fruit with full attention: the spray of scent, the sound, the stickiness on your fingers. Then eat it slowly.
Hold a warm drink with both hands and feel the heat travel into your palms before taking a sip.
Take a different route somewhere familiar. Unfamiliar streets pull your attention into the present without any effort.
Before eating, look at your plate for a few seconds. Colours, shapes, steam. Then begin.
When someone is speaking to you, quietly register the colour of their eyes. It keeps you looking at them rather than past them.
Lie on the floor for three minutes and feel every point where your body touches it. Heels, shoulders, the back of the head.
Do one thing at the speed it actually needs, not the speed your worry wants. Walking to the bus, writing a message, anything.
Pick a single song you love and follow just the bass line, or one instrument, from start to finish.
Touch something with an interesting texture: bark, a wool jumper, a cold stone. Give it twenty seconds of real attention.
End one conversation without checking your phone straight afterwards. Let it settle for a minute first.
Savour one small pleasure on purpose: a biscuit, sunlight on your face, clean sheets. Name it to yourself as it happens.
In a meeting or gathering, listen to one person as if you would need to retell their point accurately later.
Spend five minutes doing nothing at all. Sit, look, breathe. If it feels uncomfortable, that is fine. Just stay.
Look back over these forty experiments. Which two felt most natural? Those are the ones worth keeping.
From here, the aim is not to add more practices but to let a few favourites become part of ordinary life.
Some days you will be on autopilot from breakfast to bedtime. That is not failure; it is simply a busy day, and tomorrow offers another way back.
Presence grows by repetition, not intensity. A few seconds of real attention, often, beats one long perfect session.
If you have drifted away from your experiments, pick the easiest one and do it once. That is enough to restart.
Busy seasons are when presence matters most and feels hardest. Shrink the practice rather than dropping it: one breath, one sip.
Have the people around you seen any change? Sometimes others feel your attention before you do.
Attach a moment of presence to something you already do daily, like unlocking your front door or switching off the light.
Stressful days pull you into the future. Gently ask yourself: what is actually happening in this room, right now?
Being here for difficult moments counts too. Presence is not only for sunsets; it also means staying with a hard conversation.
If a practice has started to feel stale, change one detail. A new route, a new sound, a new object to study.
Looking ahead is still useful. Plan when it is time to plan, then return to whatever is in front of you.
Think of a moment from this month you were fully present for. How does that memory compare with the blurry ones?
Holidays, weekends and celebrations can still be rushed through. Before your next one, decide on one moment to savour on purpose.
Impatience will still visit. When it does, feel where it sits in your body, and let your shoulders drop a little.
Share one of your favourite small practices with a friend. Explaining it can deepen it for you as well.
Some weeks the phone will win more often. Rather than scolding yourself, move it a little further away and begin again.
Slowing down at work does not have to mean doing less. Often it means fewer mistakes and less doing things twice.
When it feels as if life is passing you by, the remedy is small: look up, breathe out, and take in one detail around you.
Children and animals live mostly in the present. If you have the chance, spend a few minutes following the pace of one.
Being present is not the same as being happy. Sometimes it means feeling tired or sad more clearly, and that is honest.
Check in on your single-tasking. Has juggling crept back? Pick one part of your day to protect again.
A good evening question: when was I most here today? Let the answer be small. A smell, a laugh, a moment of quiet.
If you missed a whole week of practice, nothing is lost. Attention is available again the moment you remember it.
Make a short list of your anchors, the small habits that bring you back. Keep it somewhere you will see it.
Listening fully is a gift that costs nothing. Who in your life might appreciate more of it this week?
Rushing ahead sometimes protects you from feeling something. If you spot that, be kind to the part of you that hurries.
Seasons change slowly. Look for one sign of that change outside, and let it remind you that life is happening now.
Compare how your days feel now with how they felt at the start. Even a slight difference is real growth.
Presence does not need these notes to continue. Your senses, your breath and your curiosity will always be there.
Choose one practice to carry forward as yours. Make it so simple you could do it on your worst day.
For ninety days you have been learning to arrive in your own life. Keep showing up for it, one ordinary moment at a time.
